title: Bread for the Rain God
sum: The chapter opens in the middle of Enki's answer to Atrahasis' plea for help against the drought. As he did against the plague (chapter 5), Enki tells Atrahasis to have the heralds order the people to stop honoring their own gods and bring all their gifts to one god, this time Adad, who holds back the rain. Bread and flour will shame Adad into sending dew by night and mist by morning, and the field will bear ninefold. The plan works.

But the people recover, and so does their noise. Before three shars of years have passed (10,800 years in the late copy), Enlil calls the gods together again and locks the whole world: Anu and Adad guard the sky, Sin and Nergal the earth, and Enki the bolt of the sea with his hairy ones. An Assyrian copy then tells the famine that follows, down to mothers and daughters starving in the street.
readings: Read as a story of clever worship
Enki's trick shows how the first hearers thought about religion: the gods can be steered by gifts, and the wise man knows which god to feed. The text never asks which god is good or true.
Read as a story of rising pressure

The chapter repeats the plague episode almost word for word with Adad in Namtar's place. The repetition builds tension. Each rescue only brings back the noise, and each time Enlil tightens his grip, until nothing is left but the Flood.

views.C: A Christian reads Enki's 'worship one god' as the opposite of the first commandment: not loyalty to the true God but a bribe to the useful one. The Bible's God gives rain to the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45) and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17); its droughts call people to turn back to him (Amos 4:7-8), not to find the right god to pay. The locking of sky, earth and sea recalls Genesis 7:11 and 8:2, where one God opens and shuts both.
views.H: The chapter is built from the Late Babylonian copy be (published by George and Al-Rawi in 1996), the Neo-Assyrian fragment Q (Sm. 292) for its first lines, and the Old Babylonian copies B and D, with the Middle Babylonian copies X and Y from Babylon and the Assyrian copy S+T for the end. SEAL notes where the late scribes misread older lines (7:13-14), swapped a rare word (ninefold for twins, 7:24), and reassigned Enlil's post to Sin and Nergal (7:73). The famine lines 7:80-103 are an Assyrian expansion.
views.M: Gods lived in temples as in houses, with doors and tables; feeding them bread and flour was the heart of worship. Adad brought storms and rain; Sin was the moon; Nergal ruled the underworld; Nisaba was grain. The world had three levels, sky, earth and the waters below, each in a god's charge, and a bolt held back the sea.
views.S: Christian readers differ on what stands behind the nations' gods. Justin Martyr held that evil demons had shown themselves to people, who, not knowing they were demons, "called them gods" (First Apology 5); read that way, Enki's advice pictures powers that trade favors for worship (1 Corinthians 10:20). Michael Heiser reads the "gods" of Psalm 82 as divine beings set over the nations and judged by God. The Psalms also call the idols nothing, "something human hands have made" (Psalm 115:4), and the rain is God's gift whoever is thanked for it (Hosea 2:8).
views.J: Jewish and Christian writers knew this kind of worship around them. Hosea accused Israel of thanking Baal for grain the LORD had given (Hosea 2:8), and Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel was fought over who sends rain (1 Kings 18). Justin Martyr later argued that the gods of the nations were demons who had made people serve them (First Apology 5).

deep.b: Enki's advice in 7:9-24 and its fulfilment in 7:44-58 repeat, line for line, his advice against the plague in Tablet I (5:34-81), with Adad in place of Namtar. Repetition is how this poem moves: commands are given, repeated by the messenger and then carried out in the same words. The reader learns to expect it, so that the small changes stand out: a new god to bribe, a new number of years, a lock on the world instead of a single plague.

deep.h: How Tablet II is pieced together
deep.b:
No single copy of Tablet II survives whole. SEAL arranges the pieces in story order as segments A to I and lists the copies: Old Babylonian (B from Sippar, written by Ipiq-Aya; D in Istanbul; H; I in the British Museum; C0 and D0 in the Schøyen collection), Middle Babylonian (X and Y from Babylon), Late Babylonian (be from Sippar) and Neo-Assyrian (Q and S+T). This chapter is SEAL's segment E, lines 1-78y. Where the copy that keeps most of a line is broken and another copy keeps the words, the Plain follows the other copy, and one variant entry for each such run of lines says which copy.

In this chapter, 7:2-8 come from Q alone; 7:9-20 from be and Q; 7:21-31 from be; 7:32-61 from the Old Babylonian B and D with be; 7:62-68 from be; 7:69-79 from the Middle Babylonian X and Y with be; and 7:80-103 from the Assyrian copy S+T alone.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two kinds of 'one god'
deep.b: Enki's 'worship Adad alone' and Elijah's 'If the LORD is the God, go after him' (1 Kings 18:21) look alike on the surface. Both come in a drought, and both end with rain. But Elijah's test asks who is real, and the answer is fire from heaven and then rain from the one God; Enki's plan asks who can be paid, and the answer is a god shamed by bread. The Carmel story can be read as the Bible's answer to the whole Near Eastern way of praying for rain that this chapter shows. This is my reading. Neither SEAL's commentary nor Millard's article, the studies this part draws on, makes the link.

echoes: Genesis 6:1; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:2; Leviticus 26:19-29; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 28:53-57; 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:21-45; Psalm 50:12-13; Job 38:8-11; Jeremiah 14:22; Hosea 2:8; Amos 4:6-8; Haggai 1:10-11; Matthew 5:45; Acts 14:17

settings.when: as the drought sent by Enlil goes on, after Atrahasis cries to him
settings.why: To show Atrahasis how to end the drought without openly defying the other gods: stop all other worship and overwhelm Adad with gifts until he must answer with rain.
settings.readers: The Old Babylonian copies are broken here. The speech survives in be, a Late Babylonian copy from Sippar, and its first lines also in Q, a Neo-Assyrian fragment (Sm. 292): its readers were the scribes of those later ages who still copied the old poem.

settings.what: Atrahasis repeats the advice to the elders
settings.to: the elders of his town, gathered at his house
settings.why: To turn the god's secret advice into a public order, given by heralds in the whole land. The wise man acts through the town's leaders.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: these lines stood in Ipiq-Aya's copy B, written at Sippar in the 11th year of Ammi-saduqa of Babylon (about 1628 BC, as SEAL dates the year name), and in the Old Babylonian copy D, which keep 7:32-43 between them. The Late Babylonian copy be from Sippar keeps the whole speech and alone has 7:27-31.

settings.what: Enlil's order to lock the world
settings.to: the gods, his sons, in assembly
settings.when: when humans have grown many and noisy again
settings.why: To cut off every source of food: rain above, water below, fish from the sea. Each god is made responsible for his part, which is why Enki will later be blamed when the fish get out (chapter 9).
settings.readers: Later scribes who kept copying the poem: the Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon (copies X and Y) and the Late Babylonian scribes of Sippar (copy be). The Old Babylonian copies are broken here.

title: Six Years of Hunger
sum: Atrahasis goes out of the city to the river, weeping day after day and bringing incense. At midnight he makes an offering, lets the river carry his gift down to Enki in the Apsu, and asks for a dream. Enki hears and sends his hairy ones across the sea to ask for news of his land; Atrahasis bows to the ground before them. Enki's minister Usmu brings word back.

Then the famine is told year by year: the old grain eaten, the storehouse opened, faces darkened, bodies shrunk, mothers and daughters sold, and in the sixth year children served up for food. One Old Babylonian copy adds that Enki heard and wept. Atrahasis' last message is bitter: the land's god has turned against it, his own god has left him, and he asks to go down to live with Enki. The Assyrian tablet ends here. A broken column, placed here only tentatively, shows Atrahasis gathering the elders once more.
readings: The chapter is mostly about how a man reaches his god: incense, tears, a river, a dream, messengers. It shows what prayer meant to its first hearers, and how unsure they were that it worked (8:45).

The six years are told with the details of real famine: hoarded food, sold children, shrunken bodies, cannibalism. The same horrors appear in the Bible's laments for Samaria and Jerusalem (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10).

views.C: A Christian reads Atrahasis' tears with sympathy: he is a man of prayer who intercedes for his people. But his god must be reached by river and messenger, and is not sure to hear; the Bible's God "knows the things you have need of before you ever ask him" (Matthew 6:8). The famine's horrors match the Bible's own, but the reason differs. In the Bible famine is a warning against evil meant to bring people back (Amos 4:6-9); here it is a way to make humans quiet. And while Enki weeps but cannot act openly, the God who grieves in Genesis 6:6 is also the Judge and the Savior.
views.H: The chapter is assembled from seven copies (D, H, I, X, Y, be and S+T), and they disagree in many small ways (river or canal, opened or used up). SEAL places the Old Babylonian copy I's tender lines on Enki's tears (8:100-105) where D, H and the Assyrian copy skip them. The Assyrian copy S+T ends its tablet at 8:121 with a catchline and the colophon 'Palace of Ashurbanipal'. Segment F (8:122-137) is placed here only tentatively.
views.M: A Babylonian looked to a personal god, 'his god', for help with the great gods. Prayer went with incense, offerings and tears, and answers were sought in dreams after sacrifice. Enki lived in the Apsu, the fresh water below, so a river could carry a gift to him. Gods had ministers (Usmu for Enki, Nusku for Enlil) and servants such as the hairy lahmu.
views.S: The Bible's angels are also sent to those who pray (Daniel 10:12; Hebrews 1:14), but the lahmu serve one god against the others and accept a man's bow, while an angel in Revelation refuses worship (Revelation 22:9). Augustine answered the pagan philosophers who taught that spirits carry people's prayers to the gods and bring back the gods' help: he held such spirits to be fallen, "most eager to inflict harm" (City of God 8.22). Read that way, messengers who carry a gift down to a god and accept worship are no friends of the one who prays.
views.J: The Bible's famines echo these lines: seven years in Egypt (Genesis 41), parents eating children in Samaria and Jerusalem (2 Kings 6:28-29; Lamentations 4:10), children sold for debt in Nehemiah's day (Nehemiah 5:5). Daniel's prayer by the Tigris and the messenger who came because his words were heard (Daniel 10:2-12) is the nearest biblical scene to Atrahasis by the river.

deep.b: The report in 8:69-99 counts six years. In the first the people ate the old grain (8:77); in the second they broke open the storehouse (8:78); in the third hunger darkened their faces and bent their bodies (8:79-85); in the fourth they shrank further (8:86-87); in the fifth mothers hoarded food and families were sold for silver (8:88-92); in the sixth children were eaten (8:93-95). SEAL reads the scales of the fifth year as a sale into slavery and the sixth year as the coming of cannibalism, and the Bible's own records tell of both (Nehemiah 5:2-5; 2 Kings 6:25-29).

The speakers are not marked in the Akkadian and some lines are broken. SEAL reads it this way: Enki sends his minister Usmu to Atrahasis (8:57-60); Usmu speaks to Atrahasis (8:61-68); then, from 8:69, Usmu reports back to Enki what Atrahasis told him about the famine (the Old Babylonian copy D marks reported speech with the particle -mi, and the late copy be draws a dividing line). The Plain follows that reading with its quotation marks.

8:1-4 come from the Middle and Late Babylonian copies X, Y and be, the Old Babylonian D and the Assyrian S+T; 8:5-16 mostly from D (with X, Y and be at 8:6-7 and S+T at 8:13-14); 8:17-37 from D, X and be; 8:38-56 from the Old Babylonian I with X and be; 8:57-68 from be alone; 8:69-87 from D, H, I and be (with S+T from 8:78); 8:88-99 from S+T alone; 8:100-106 from I alone; 8:107-113 from D, H and S+T; 8:114-121 from S+T alone; and segment F (8:122-137) from I. Where one copy is broken and another keeps the words, a variant entry for the run says which copy the Plain follows.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the intercessor before the Flood
deep.b: Genesis gives Noah no words before the Flood; he simply does what God says (Genesis 6:22). Atrahasis, by contrast, weeps, prays and pleads for his land for years. 2 Peter calls Noah "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5). I suggest that Atrahasis shows how the ancient world already imagined the Flood's survivor as a man who stood between his people and heaven, a role the Bible gives in full to Abraham and Moses (Genesis 18:23-32; Exodus 32:11-14) and, finally, to Christ. This is my own reading, not a claim about borrowing.

echoes: Genesis 5:24; Genesis 6:6; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 8:1; Genesis 41:35-36; Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57; 1 Kings 3:5; 2 Kings 6:28-29; Nehemiah 5:5; Psalm 22:1; Psalm 141:2; Lamentations 4:10; Daniel 10:2-12; Amos 4:6-9; Matthew 6:8; Luke 19:41; Revelation 6:5-6; Revelation 22:8-9

settings.to: the river, and through it Enki, his lord
settings.when: at midnight, after his offering, as sleep comes on him
settings.why: To get his gift and his plea down to Enki in the Apsu, and to ask for an answer in a dream.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils, in the copy D (copy I keeps 8:21 too), and later the Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon (copy X) and the Late Babylonian scribes of Sippar (copy be), who copied the same prayer.

settings.why: To get news of his land and bring back the man's message.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils (copy D), and later the Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon (copy X) and the Late Babylonian scribes of Sippar (copy be).

settings.when: when the messengers reach the quay of the Apsu
settings.why: To assure Atrahasis that his prayer reached Enki by the river, and to receive his answer.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: the Old Babylonian copy I keeps the most of this exchange. The Middle Babylonian copy X from Babylon and the Late Babylonian copy be from Sippar keep much of it too.

settings.what: Usmu's message and the report of the famine
settings.to: Atrahasis, and then (from 8:69) Enki, as SEAL reads it
settings.why: To carry Enki's word to Atrahasis and Atrahasis' account of the six years of hunger back to Enki.
settings.readers: The Late Babylonian scribes of Sippar (copy be) for 8:59-71; then Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils (copies D, H and I, with be) for 8:69-87; and the Assyrian scribes of Ashurbanipal's palace (copy S+T), whose copy alone keeps 8:88-99.
views: SEAL takes 8:69-99 as Usmu's report to Enki of Atrahasis' words, marked by the particle -mi in D.
Because the speaker is not named, the lines can also be read as continuing the speech that began at 8:62.

settings.when: after the lost lines in which Enki answered him
settings.why: To complain that the land's god has turned against it and that Enki has left him, and to ask to live with Enki in the Apsu.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils (copies D and H, for 8:110-113), and the Assyrian scribes of Ashurbanipal's palace (copy S+T), whose copy alone keeps 8:115-118.

title: The Oath of the Flood
sum: When the text resumes, the famine seems to have ended. Enlil, furious, reminds the gods that they all swore to keep their posts, and accuses Enki: wherever he went, he untied the yoke, set up a release and let loose the fish of the sea for the people. Through messengers and then face to face, Enki answers that he did his part; the sea's two gatekeepers broke the great bolt, the fish escaped, and he punished them.

Enlil then calls the whole assembly to swear to the flood, and the gods swear, Anu first. Plenty returns for a time, and Enki sits in the council, troubled, while 'laughter' (or 'vexation') eats at him. A speech recalling the making of humankind proposes to bind Enki by oath too. He refuses: 'Should I bring my hand down on my own people?' He leaves the work of the flood to others and names its gods. Tablet II ends: 'Enlil has done an evil work against the people,' and Ipiq-Aya signs and dates his copy.
readings: Enlil accuses, Enki defends himself, witnesses are named, a penalty is laid on the guilty gatekeepers, and the assembly swears an oath. The Flood is decided in a court of gods.

Genesis tells the same moment, the decision to send the Flood, in a few verses: God sees human evil, grieves, decides, and makes a covenant with Noah (Genesis 6:5-18). The poem needs a quarrel between gods, an oath and a refusal to reach the same point.

views.C: For a Christian the chapter's sharpest line is its last: a voice whose speaker is lost calls the flood decree "an evil work against the people" (9:168), and the tablet ends without an answer. The Bible's one God sends the Flood because "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:11), grieves to do it (Genesis 6:6), saves Noah in the same breath (Genesis 6:17-18), and afterward swears never to do it again (Isaiah 54:9). Judging and saving belong to one just God.
views.H: The chapter joins the Old Babylonian copies D, H, I, C0 (the Schøyen tablet published by Andrew George in 2009) and Ipiq-Aya's own B (9:134-176) with the Middle Babylonian copy X, which alone keeps the round trips of the messengers and the oath scene (9:38-80). SEAL lists the parallels of 9:147-151 with the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, lines 100-103, and corrects several older readings (the two companions, 9:24; Malukku, 9:122; 'evil', 9:166). Millard held that the Flood story was taken into the Gilgamesh cycle with some editing, a case where "literary borrowing cannot be doubted".
views.M: The gods rule by assembly and oath, like a city's council. An oath sworn by the gods binds them; that is why Enlil wants Enki under oath and why, in Tablet III, Enki speaks to a wall instead of to a man. Each god keeps a post (sky, earth, sea), and gods have ministers, messengers and lesser gods to do their work.
views.S: Michael Heiser reads the "gods" of Psalm 82 as divine beings who rule the nations and are judged by God for injustice; read that way, the council of 9:77-80 is a picture of such powers with no one above them. Heiser also sets out the other readings of Psalm 82's "gods", as human rulers and judges. Either way the Bible's heavenly court answers to one Judge (Psalm 82:1, 8).
views.J: Berossus, the Babylonian priest who wrote in Greek, retold Babylon's history from creation to the Flood (the Babyloniaca of Berossus); George links the rare word malukku (9:122) to a name in his account. Jewish writers told of the Watchers' sin as the cause of the Flood (1 Enoch 6-10), placing the evil among rebel spirits and humans, never in God.

deep.b: Enlil's charge comes three times (9:14-21, 9:28-37, 9:106-111), and Enki's answer comes three times (9:47-59, 9:64-75, 9:114-123). The answers grow clearer: the Old Babylonian copy C0 names the culprits, the two gatekeepers Malukku and the Sea (9:122), while the Middle Babylonian copy X has Enki say he killed the guards of the sea, which SEAL thinks is a misunderstanding of that line (9:55). Either way Enki never says he meant to help the people, though he had wept for them (8:100-102).

Enki's refusal names the gods who will do the work: Shullat and Hanish going ahead, Errakal tearing out the posts, another god opening the dams, the throne-bearer leading on, the waters spilling over (9:147-152). SEAL lists these lines as parallel to the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, lines 100-103, and notes that Shullat and Hanish are named in line 99 of that tablet, also with the flood. The poem's Flood is the work of many gods, set for "the moon's day" (9:155), which SEAL reads as the day of the new moon.

9:1-27 come from the Old Babylonian copy D, with H from 9:15; 9:28-37 from D, H and I, with the Middle Babylonian X; 9:38-80 almost wholly from X (D keeps parts of 9:55-59); 9:81-86 from D; 9:87-127 from C0 and D (C0 alone for 9:114-127); 9:128-151 from D and Ipiq-Aya's B, with C0 from 9:139; 9:152-163 from C0; 9:165-170 from D and B; and the scribe's count and colophon (9:171-176) from B alone. Where one copy is broken and another keeps the words, a variant entry for the run says which copy the Plain follows.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the oath reversed
deep.b: Tablet II of Atrahasis ends with an oath to destroy (9:78-80) and a god who will not take it (9:140-141). The Bible ends its Flood with an oath to spare: "as I swore that Noah's waters / would never again sweep over the earth" (Isaiah 54:9). If Genesis was written for people who knew stories like this one, God's oath after the Flood would have read as a direct answer: heaven's council once swore to drown humankind; the LORD swears never again, and seals it with the bow in the clouds (Genesis 9:12-17). This is my reading. Others have compared the whole outline of Genesis 1-9 with Atrahasis (see the topic ancient-near-east).

echoes: Genesis 3:12; Genesis 6:5-18; Genesis 7:11; Genesis 9:11-15; Genesis 18:25; Job 38:8-11; Psalm 2:4; Psalm 29:3-10; Psalm 82:1-8; Psalm 104:10-15; Isaiah 54:9-10; Ezekiel 33:11; Mark 4:39-41; Luke 4:18; John 6:11; Hebrews 6:13

settings.to: the assembly of the great gods
settings.when: after Enki's release of the fish has ended the famine
settings.why: To accuse Enki of breaking the gods' shared oath by freeing the people from hunger.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils, in the copies D and H. These lines also stood in Ipiq-Aya's tablet B, which held all 439 lines of Tablet II, but that part of it is lost.

settings.what: Enlil summons the two companions and repeats the charge
settings.to: Nusku, then the two companions (probably Shullat and Hanish) sent to Enki
settings.why: To send the accusation to Enki by messengers.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils (copies D, H and I), and the Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon (copy X), whose copy alone keeps the messengers' trips that follow (9:38-75).

settings.to: Enlil's messengers, and through them Enlil
settings.why: To clear himself: he kept his post, but the gatekeepers of the sea broke the bolt, and he punished them.
settings.readers: The Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon: this form of the defense survives in copy X (the Old Babylonian D keeps parts of 9:55-59).

settings.to: the assembly of all the gods
settings.why: To bind every god to the flood, so that no one could undo it as Enki undid the famine.
settings.readers: The Middle Babylonian scribes of Babylon: only copy X keeps these lines.

settings.what: Enlil and Enki face to face
settings.when: after Enki's distress in the council
settings.why: Enlil repeats the charge; Enki answers that each god kept the post given him by all, and names the gatekeepers who failed.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: D keeps Enlil's charge (9:106-111) and the Schøyen copy C0 Enki's answer (9:113-123).

settings.when: after Enki names the gatekeepers who failed
settings.why: To answer Enki's defense. Only the first words survive ('It is you who ...'), so what Enlil said is lost.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: only the Schøyen copy C0 keeps these lines.

settings.what: A speech recalling the making of humankind
settings.by: probably the birth goddess Mami, as SEAL thinks
settings.why: To remind the gods of the work they put on humankind and of the slain god, and to propose binding Enki by oath.
views: SEAL: the lines repeat Mami's speech in Tablet I (3:73-79), so she is the likely speaker. SEAL adds that Enki's reply (9:139) is to the whole assembly of the gods, not to Mami alone.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: D keeps these lines, and Ipiq-Aya's copy B the last of them (9:134-137).

settings.when: when they try to bind him by oath
settings.why: To refuse to raise his hand against his own people, to leave the flood to Enlil, and to name the gods who will bring it.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: Ipiq-Aya's copy B and D keep 9:140-151, and the Schøyen copy C0 keeps most of the rest.

settings.by: a speaker whose name is lost
settings.to: more than one hearer (the verb is plural), perhaps the assembly named in 9:165
settings.when: at the end of Tablet II
settings.why: To say what the gods have done: ordered total destruction, an evil work against the people.
settings.readers: Old Babylonian scribes and their pupils: Ipiq-Aya's copy B and D keep these lines, and B goes on with the scribe's count and his colophon (9:171-176).
